lead: Hybrid (h) parameters take the input current I₁ and the output voltage V₂ as the free variables, and give the input voltage V₁ and the output current I₂. One free variable is a current and the other a voltage, so the four constants have mixed units: one in ohms, one in siemens and two plain ratios. That mix fits a transistor amplifier, whose input is driven by a base current and whose output sits across a collector voltage, which is why transistor data sheets quote h parameters. The inverse hybrid (g) set swaps the roles and takes V₁ and I₂ as the free pair.
prereq: You need the port variables and their directions, Z and Y parameters and dependent sources.

blocks.text: V₁ = h₁₁I₁ + h₁₂V₂,   I₂ = h₂₁I₁ + h₂₂V₂
blocks.where: where both currents enter their ports, as everywhere in this unit; in matrix form [V₁; I₂] = [h][I₁; V₂].

blocks.text: The equations draw a simple model. The first is KVL at the input: a resistance h₁₁ carrying I₁, in series with a dependent voltage source h₁₂V₂ fed back from the output. The second is KCL at the output: a dependent current source h₂₁I₁ in parallel with a conductance h₂₂. This is the h-parameter equivalent circuit of the figure, and it is the small-signal model of a bipolar transistor.
Each parameter is a ratio with one free variable set to zero: V₂ = 0 means the output is shorted, I₁ = 0 means the input is open.

In transistor work the four numbers carry letter names: h<sub>i</sub> (input), h<sub>r</sub> (reverse), h<sub>f</sub> (forward) and h<sub>o</sub> (output), with a second letter for the configuration, so h<sub>ie</sub>, h<sub>re</sub>, h<sub>fe</sub>, h<sub>oe</sub> in common emitter. With I₂ entering the collector, h<sub>fe</sub> = β is positive. h<sub>re</sub> is small, of the order of 10⁻⁴, and is often neglected.

From the Z equations, short-circuiting the output (V₂ = 0) gives I₂ = −(z₂₁/z₂₂)I₁ and V₁ = (Δz/z₂₂)I₁; opening the input gives V₁ = (z₁₂/z₂₂)V₂ and I₂ = V₂/z₂₂. So h₁₁ = Δz/z₂₂, h₁₂ = z₁₂/z₂₂, h₂₁ = −z₂₁/z₂₂ and h₂₂ = 1/z₂₂. For a passive network h₁₂ is positive and h₂₁ negative, and a reciprocal network has h₁₂ = −h₂₁.
I₁ = g₁₁V₁ + g₁₂I₂,   V₂ = g₂₁V₁ + g₂₂I₂
blocks.where: where g₁₁ = I₁/V₁ with I₂ = 0 (siemens), g₁₂ = I₁/I₂ with V₁ = 0, g₂₁ = V₂/V₁ with I₂ = 0, and g₂₂ = V₂/I₂ with V₁ = 0 (ohms).

blocks.text: The g matrix is the inverse of the h matrix, [g] = [h]⁻¹:
g₁₁ = h₂₂/Δh,  g₁₂ = −h₁₂/Δh,  g₂₁ = −h₂₁/Δh,  g₂₂ = h₁₁/Δh
blocks.where: where Δh = h₁₁h₂₂ − h₁₂h₂₁ is dimensionless (ohms × siemens). The same pattern with g and h swapped gives h from g.

blocks.text: The g set suits a voltage amplifier model: g₂₁ is the open-circuit voltage gain, as in an op-amp stage. g₂₂ is an impedance and h₂₂ an admittance; they are not reciprocals of each other, because only whole matrices invert.

spec.aria: An equivalent circuit: at the input a 1 kilo-ohm resistor h11 in series with a diamond voltage source h12 V2 = minus 0.01 V; at the output a diamond current source h21 I1 = 0.5 mA in parallel with 50 kilo-ohm 1 over h22. I1 = 10 microamps, V2 = minus 5 V, I2 = 0.4 mA.

examples.question: A transistor at its bias point has h₁₁ = 1 kΩ, h₁₂ = 0.002, h₂₁ = 50 and h₂₂ = 20 μS. The input current is I₁ = 10 μA and the output port sits at V₂ = −5 V. Find V₁ and I₂, and the load resistance that produces this V₂.
steps: Base units: h₁₁ = 1000 Ω, h₂₂ = 20 × 10⁻⁶ S, I₁ = 10 × 10⁻⁶ A, V₂ = −5 V.
Input drop: h₁₁I₁ = 1000 × 10 × 10⁻⁶ = 0.01 V. Feedback term: h₁₂V₂ = 0.002 × (−5) = −0.01 V.
V₁ = 0.01 + (−0.01) = 0 V. The two terms cancel exactly for these numbers.
Controlled source: h₂₁I₁ = 50 × 10 × 10⁻⁶ = 0.5 mA. Output conductance term: h₂₂V₂ = 20 × 10⁻⁶ × (−5) = −0.1 mA.
A passive load obeys V₂ = −I₂R<sub>L</sub>, so R<sub>L</sub> = −V₂/I₂ = 5/(0.4 × 10⁻³) = 12.5 kΩ. The negative V₂ is simply the inverting output of the amplifier across its load.
examples.answer: V₁ = 0 V, I₂ = 0.4 mA, and the load is 12.5 kΩ.

examples.question: Find the h parameters of the T network with Z₁ = 2 Ω, Z₂ = 3 Ω and Z₃ = 4 Ω (z₁₁ = 6 Ω, z₁₂ = z₂₁ = 4 Ω, z₂₂ = 7 Ω) directly from the circuit, and check them against the Z-to-h formulas.
steps: Output shorted (V₂ = 0): port 1 sees Z₁ + Z₂ ∥ Z₃ = 2 + 12/7 = 3.7143 Ω, so h₁₁ = 3.7143 Ω.
In the same test I₁ divides between Z₃ and Z₂ (the short). The current through Z₂ is I₁ × Z₃/(Z₂ + Z₃) = (4/7)I₁, leaving terminal 2, so I₂ = −(4/7)I₁ and h₂₁ = −0.5714.
Input open (I₁ = 0): drive V₂. Current V₂/(Z₂ + Z₃) = V₂/7 flows through Z₂ and Z₃, so h₂₂ = 1/7 = 0.1429 S.
No current in Z₁, so V₁ equals the voltage across Z₃: V₁ = 4 × V₂/7, giving h₁₂ = 0.5714.
Check with the formulas: Δz/z₂₂ = 26/7 = 3.7143 Ω ✓; z₁₂/z₂₂ = 4/7 ✓; −z₂₁/z₂₂ = −4/7 ✓; 1/z₂₂ = 1/7 S ✓. Also h₁₂ = −h₂₁, as a reciprocal network needs.

traps: h₁₁ needs the output shorted (V₂ = 0), not open. For the T network the open-output value would be z₁₁ = 6 Ω, not h₁₁ = 3.7143 Ω.
Only h₁₁ (ohms) and h₂₂ (siemens) have units. h₁₂ and h₂₁ are pure numbers; writing h₂₂ in ohms or h₁₂ in volts loses the mark.
Do not drop h₁₂V₂ unless the question says so. In the transistor example it cancels the whole input drop.
A passive network has h₂₁ < 0 with the entering convention (−4/7 for the T network). A transistor has h₂₁ = +β because its dependent source pushes current into the collector terminal.
One test gives only two parameters: the output-short test gives h₁₁ and h₂₁; h₁₂ and h₂₂ need the input open.

quiz.q: Which two variables are the free variables of the h set, and which of the g set?
quiz.a: h: I₁ and V₂ (giving V₁ and I₂). g: V₁ and I₂ (giving I₁ and V₂).

quiz.q: State the unit and test condition of each h parameter.
quiz.a: h₁₁ (Ω) and h₂₁ (none) with the output shorted; h₁₂ (none) and h₂₂ (S) with the input open.

quiz.q: Why are h parameters the natural choice for a bipolar transistor?
quiz.a: Its input is low-impedance and current-driven, and its output is high-impedance, so I₁ and V₂ are the easy variables to set; a short across the output and an open input are easy to make at the bias point, and h₂₁ is then the current gain β.

quiz.q: A two-port has h₁₁ = 2 kΩ, h₁₂ = 0, h₂₁ = 100, h₂₂ = 50 μS. With I₁ = 20 μA and V₂ = 0, find V₁ and I₂.
quiz.a: V₁ = 2000 × 20 × 10⁻⁶ = 0.04 V; I₂ = 100 × 20 × 10⁻⁶ = 2 mA. The h₁₂ and h₂₂ terms vanish because V₂ = 0.

quiz.q: A two-port has g₁₁ = 1 mS, g₁₂ = 0, g₂₁ = −2 and g₂₂ = 500 Ω. Find h₁₁ and h₂₂.
Find the g parameters of the T network from its h parameters (h₁₁ = 26/7 Ω, h₁₂ = 4/7, h₂₁ = −4/7, h₂₂ = 1/7 S).
A student measures h₁₂ with the output shorted and reads zero. What went wrong?
quiz.a: h₁₂ = V₁/V₂ needs the input open and port 2 driven. With the output shorted V₂ = 0, so the ratio has no meaning. Open port 1, apply V₂ and measure the voltage at port 1.

beyond: Not for the exam. The h model is the low-frequency form of the hybrid-π transistor model that simulators use; at higher frequency its parameters become complex and frequency-dependent. Data sheets of small-signal transistors still list h<sub>fe</sub> and h<sub>ie</sub> at a stated collector current. Search for “hybrid-pi model” and “h parameter transistor amplifier analysis”.
